title: Extending without editing
idea: The Open/Closed Principle (OCP) says a class should be open for extension and closed for modification: new behaviour arrives as new code, not edits.

analogy.text: A power strip takes a new lamp, charger or fan without rewiring the wall. The socket shape stays fixed; what you plug in varies.
analogy.breaks: Socket shapes rarely change; your interface sometimes must, and that costs.

points: Closed means tested callers stay untouched when a new variant arrives.
Open means the variant ships as a new class behind an existing interface.
Use it where variants keep arriving: payment methods, discounts, file formats, alert channels.
In interviews, name the interface where tomorrow's requirement will plug in.

hero.title: A new method plugs in, nothing reopens

steps.caption: `FeeCalculator` knows only `PaymentMethod`. It finds a method by key and asks it for the fee.
Card and bank each own their rule: a percentage plus a fixed part, or one flat fee.
Wallets arrive as `CappedPercent`, a brand-new class. No existing file is reopened.
`PaymentFeeDemo` passes one more method to the constructor. Wiring is the only place that learns about wallets.
An unknown key throws instead of falling to a default price, so a missing method fails loudly.
The calculator and its tests are unchanged. That already-tested code is exactly what "closed" protects.

code.title: The problem
code.caption: An `if` chain per method. A new menu entry nobody wired in is charged the card fee.

walk.text: This class must be reopened for every new payment method, forever.
Each method is a branch, so every fee change edits and retests this one method.
The last line doubles as a default. A missing branch is not an error, only a wrong fee.
Product added wallet to the menu. It pays 3.20 instead of 0.99, and nothing fails.

code.title: The fix
code.caption: One interface, one class per method. Wallets are a new class plus one wiring line.

walk.text: `PaymentMethod` is the extension point: a key and the fee rule for it.
Card and bank are separate records. The card record validates its numbers at construction.
`CappedPercent` is the new variant: 1% capped at 99 cents. Adding it touched no existing class.
The calculator indexes methods by key and rejects duplicate keys at construction.
A map lookup replaces the `if` chain. Unknown keys throw instead of borrowing another fee.
Main wires three methods, prices each one and shows an unknown key being rejected.

pitfalls: A catch-all `else` or default hides a missing variant; throw `IllegalArgumentException` instead.
Interfaces for things that never vary add files, not flexibility; wait for the second variant.
Changing the interface reopens every implementation; keep extension points small and stable.

quiz.q: Next sprint brings a fourth method, buy now pay later. With the fixed design, what changes?
options: A new PaymentMethod and one wiring line
quiz.why: The calculator only looks methods up by key. Main passes in one more `PaymentMethod`, a new class or another configured record; tested classes stay closed.

takeaway: Add new behaviour as a new class; leave tested code closed.
